passages.title: Community Reading Club · Original A2 Practice Text
passages.text: A community center in East Bay has started a free reading club for teenagers. The program began in February and meets every Wednesday from four to five in the afternoon. The center first planned to meet on Fridays, but it changed the day after several students reported that they had sports practice then. Members meet in Room B, beside the small garden. They read short stories and discuss the characters in groups. The center provides printed stories, but participants should bring a notebook and a pen. New members do not need to buy books. However, they must complete a simple registration form before attending their first meeting. The form asks for a name and a contact method; it does not ask for school exam scores. The club currently has eighteen registered members. A volunteer teacher leads the discussion, and two older students help prepare the room. Last month, the group invited a local writer to describe how she planned her stories. The notice says the writer answered questions after her talk. It does not say that she will return next month. The center plans to add a second group if enough students register, but it has not announced a date for that change. The director also asked students to suggest new stories for future meetings. Suggestions can be written on a small card and placed in a box by the entrance. No story has been selected for the next meeting.

passages.title: Student Repair Workshop · Original B1 Practice Text
passages.text: Riverside Vocational School runs a small repair workshop where students learn to fix everyday objects. The workshop opens to visitors on the first Saturday of each month. Visitors can bring a bicycle light, a broken bag strap, or another simple item for the students to examine. The students work with a teacher who checks each repair before an item is returned. The workshop does not repair mobile phones because it lacks the required equipment. During the July session, twenty-four visitors arrived between nine and eleven in the morning. Twelve brought bicycles or bicycle parts, seven brought bags, and five brought small household objects. The volunteers completed nineteen repairs that day. They explained to the remaining visitors why their items needed different tools or spare parts. A report published by the school noted that some visitors returned in August with the missing parts, but it did not say how many. The school encourages visitors to describe a problem clearly before handing over an object. This helps students decide which tools to prepare. The workshop is free for visitors; however, replacement parts are not always provided. Anyone who needs a new part must first discuss its cost with the teacher. The school hopes that the project will help students practice communication as well as technical skills. A student volunteer explained that people sometimes describe the same problem using different words. The teacher encourages learners to ask polite follow-up questions rather than assume they understand immediately. The report does not claim that every repair can be completed during one session. Some problems require more time or an additional visit.
